title: Food & Nutrition
description: Food, nutrition and healthy eating: food groups, a balanced thali, water, where food comes from, nutrients and their jobs, reading labels, food safety, and the science and culture of diets. lessons.title: Foods That Help Me Grow
objectives: Name everyday foods that help us grow
Know that sweets and fried snacks are "sometimes" foods
explanation: Food gives our body energy to play and helps us grow. Fruits and vegetables, rice, roti, dal, milk, curd, eggs and nuts are everyday foods that keep us strong.
Sweets, chips, fried snacks and fizzy drinks are "sometimes foods". They are fine as a treat, but they don't help us grow much, and too much sugar can hurt our teeth.
Eating many different colours of fruits and vegetables — like a rainbow — gives our body lots of good things.

objectives: Explain why our bodies need water

explanation: More than half of your body is water! You lose water when you sweat, breathe and go to the toilet, so you need to drink more every day.
Drink more water on hot days and when you run and play. If you feel thirsty, tired or have a headache, your body might need water.

lessons.title: Go, Grow and Glow Foods
objectives: Sort foods into energy, body-building and protective groups
Explain each group's job
explanation: Energy ("go") foods give us power to run and think: rice, roti, millets, potatoes. Body-building ("grow") foods help muscles and bones grow: dal, beans, milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish, meat and nuts.
Protective ("glow") foods keep us healthy and help fight illness: fruits and vegetables full of vitamins and minerals.
We need a little fat too, from oil, ghee or nuts, but only small amounts. Eating from all groups every day is called a balanced diet.

lessons.title: Build a Balanced Thali
objectives: Plan a balanced thali with all food groups
Compare thalis from different regions
explanation: A traditional Indian thali often includes a grain (rice or roti), a dal or other protein, vegetables (sabzi), curd, a salad and sometimes a small sweet. This can make a very balanced meal.
Thalis differ across India: a Gujarati thali may have dhokla and kadhi; a South Indian meal may have rice, sambar, rasam and poriyal; a Punjabi thali may have makki roti and sarson saag.
A good guide: about half the plate vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains, a quarter protein, with water to drink.

story.title: The Thali Tour

lessons.title: The Journey of Rice
objectives: Trace a food from farm to plate
Explain why reducing food waste matters
explanation: Rice is grown by farmers in flooded fields, harvested, threshed to remove the grains, dried, husked and polished in mills, packed, transported, sold in shops and finally cooked in our kitchens.
Many people work along this chain: farmers, labourers, mill workers, truck drivers, shopkeepers and cooks.
Wasting food wastes all their work, plus water, land and energy. Taking only what we can eat and using leftovers helps.

lessons.title: Kitchen Safety Heroes
objectives: Follow basic food hygiene rules
Recognise signs that food has spoiled
prerequisites: Knows germs can make us ill
explanation: Germs on hands and food can cause tummy illnesses. Wash hands with soap before eating and cooking. Wash fruits and vegetables with clean water.
Keep cooked food covered so flies can't land on it. Store milk, curd and leftovers in a cool place or fridge. Keep raw meat separate from food that won't be cooked.
Spoiled food may smell bad, look slimy or mouldy, or taste sour when it shouldn't. When in doubt, ask an adult — and don't eat it.

lessons.title: What Each Nutrient Does
objectives: Name the main nutrients and their functions
Identify food sources of each
explanation: Carbohydrates (grains, potatoes) are the main energy source. Proteins (dal, milk, eggs, paneer, meat, soya) build and repair the body. Fats (oils, nuts, ghee) store energy and help absorb some vitamins.

Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts: vitamin A (carrots, mangoes) for eyes; vitamin C (amla, citrus) for healing and immunity; vitamin D (sunlight, fortified milk) and calcium (milk, ragi) for bones; iron (leafy greens, jaggery, dals) for healthy blood.
Fibre (whole grains, vegetables, fruit) helps digestion. Water is needed for almost every body process.

context.text: National surveys in India have found anaemia (often linked to iron deficiency) is common among children and women, which is why iron-rich foods and supplementation programmes are promoted.

vocabulary.meaning: a substance in food that the body needs

examples: Amla is very rich in vitamin C.

story.title: Sailors and the Missing Vitamin
story.text: Centuries ago, sailors on long voyages became weak, with bleeding gums — a disease called scurvy. They had plenty of biscuits but no fresh fruit. When ships began carrying citrus fruits, scurvy disappeared. The missing nutrient was vitamin C.

units.title: Diets Around the World

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Many Ways to Eat Well
objectives: Describe different diets and food practices respectfully
Explain how each can be balanced
explanation: People eat in many ways. Vegetarians don't eat meat or fish; many eat dairy and some eat eggs. Vegans eat no animal products. Non-vegetarians eat meat, fish or eggs as well as plant foods.

Religious and cultural practices shape diets: many Jains avoid root vegetables; many Muslims eat halal food and avoid pork; many Hindus avoid beef; many Sikhs eat langar (vegetarian community meals); fasting is part of Ramadan, Navratri, Ekadashi and other observances.
Every diet can be healthy if it's balanced. Vegetarians often get protein from dals, milk, paneer and nuts; vegans may need to plan for vitamin B12, calcium and iron.

context.text: Food rules such as Jain avoidance of root vegetables (to minimise harm to living organisms) and Islamic halal requirements are religious practices that followers observe as part of their faith.

vocabulary.meaning: a diet without meat or fish

lessons.title: Decoding the Label
objectives: Read nutrition facts and ingredient lists
Compare products using per-100 g values
explanation: Packaged foods in India carry labels showing ingredients, nutrition information and an FSSAI licence number. Ingredients are listed from largest to smallest amount.
Nutrition facts often show energy (kcal), protein, carbohydrate (including sugars), fat and sodium per 100 g and per serving. Comparing per 100 g lets you compare fairly between products.
Watch for hidden sugars (sucrose, glucose syrup, maltodextrin), high salt (sodium), and trans fats. Check "best before" or "use by" dates.

lessons.title: Energy In, Energy Out
objectives: Explain energy balance in simple terms
Discuss healthy habits and positive body image
explanation: Food energy is measured in kilocalories (kcal). Our bodies use energy for everything — breathing, thinking, growing and moving. Growing children need plenty of energy.

Over time, if energy in roughly matches energy out, body weight stays fairly stable for adults; children need extra for growth. Very high-sugar, highly processed foods can make it easy to take in lots of energy with few nutrients.

Healthy bodies come in many shapes and sizes. Good habits — balanced meals, regular activity, enough sleep, and water — matter more than numbers on a scale. Teasing people about their bodies is hurtful and wrong.

vocabulary.meaning: a unit of food energy

examples: A brisk walk and a game of football both use energy.

lessons.title: Weighing Nutrition Evidence
objectives: Distinguish observational and experimental nutrition studies
Critically evaluate fad diets and supplement claims
explanation: Many nutrition studies are observational: researchers compare what people eat with their health over time. These can show associations but not prove cause, because people who eat differently also differ in other ways.
Randomised trials test diets directly but are hard to run for years. Strong conclusions come from many studies pointing the same way.

In India, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and the National Institute of Nutrition publish dietary guidelines. Fad diets promising rapid results, and supplements claiming miracle effects, rarely have strong evidence; most people can meet needs through a varied diet, though some groups need specific supplements.

examples: Iron and folic acid supplements are recommended in pregnancy.

lessons.title: The Double Burden of Malnutrition
objectives: Explain undernutrition and overnutrition
Evaluate public nutrition programmes in India
explanation: Malnutrition means poor nutrition in either direction. Undernutrition includes stunting (low height for age), wasting (low weight for height) and micronutrient deficiencies like anaemia. Overnutrition includes overweight and obesity, linked to diabetes and heart disease.
India faces a "double burden": both undernutrition and rising diet-related diseases, sometimes in the same communities.

Public programmes include Integrated Child Development Services (anganwadi centres), school meals (PM POSHAN, formerly the Mid-Day Meal scheme), the public distribution system, and fortification of foods like salt with iodine. Evaluating them involves looking at coverage, quality and outcomes.

context.text: National Family Health Survey data show substantial rates of child stunting and anaemia alongside rising adult overweight; universal salt iodisation greatly reduced iodine deficiency disorders.

vocabulary.meaning: poor nutrition from too little or too much of certain nutrients
low height for age
low weight for height
adding nutrients to common foods

examples: Iodised salt prevents goitre.

story.text: In a village school, many children used to come to class hungry. When a hot school lunch began, attendance rose and teachers noticed children concentrating better. Researchers later studied such programmes to measure how much they helped — and how to make the meals more nutritious.
